Photograph: Sergei Supinsky/AFP/Getty Images Foreign policy Burnham accuses Russia of ‘outrageous threats’ against UK as he visits Kyiv Moscow warns of increased tensions with Britain as Burnham offers Ukraine declassified details of missile components Europe live – latest updates Jessica Elgot , Kiran Stacey and Dan Sabbagh Mon 24 Aug 2026 08.07 EDT First published on Mon 24 Aug 2026 06.49 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google Andy Burnham has accused the Kremlin of “outrageous threats” against the UK as Russia warned of an escalation in tensions after the UK’s decision to present Ukraine with newly declassified blueprints to allow Kyiv to improve its production of long-range missiles. Speaking in Kyiv, Burnham compared Ukraine’s struggle to Britain’s fight against Nazi Germany. “My nation kept the flame of European freedom alive in the 20th century, you hold that flame in the 21st,” Burnham said in a speech in front of St Sophia cathedral to mark the 35th anniversary of Ukraine’s independence. “Despite Russia’s outrageous threats to my country, we will continue our support for Ukraine.” In his first trip abroad as the prime minister, Burnham will give Ukraine previously classified information on the British manufactured components for long-range cruise missiles. Vladimir Putin’s spokesperson Dmitry Peskov said the exchange would add “fuel to the fire” and scupper any moves towards a peace deal. Burnham hit back in an interview shortly after his speech. He said: “Who started the fire? That’s the question, isn’t it?” The UK prime minister will join a conference call while in Kyiv with 34 leaders in the coalition of the willing, countries that have promised to help keep Ukraine secure in the event of a truce with Russia. Moscow said it would identify and destroy the locations of missile production sites. “Britain is involved in this war on the side of the Kyiv regime,” Peskov told reporters. “Britain methodically and regularly adds fuel ‌to the fire, and methodically and regularly hatches schemes to prevent even the slightest progress in the peaceful settlement process.” Kyiv was braced for another wave of Russian missile attacks as it marked Independence Day on Monday, attended by other European leaders alongside Burnham. As Russian missiles rain down on Kyiv, casualties mount and the mood darkens Read more The prime minister’s decision to declassify the information about the UK-made components of the Storm Shadow/Scalp missiles will enable Ukraine to eventually build its own version, though this may take years. In his speech, Burnham said Ukraine had “endured 12 years of naked aggression, the occupation of Crimea, and now four and a half years of Russia’s full-scale invasion, all aimed at crushing the independence that we are here to celebrate.” He said: “Russia’s actions have not changed the path this nation is on. It’s confirmed it. You have stood tall and defiant in the face of everything Russia has thrown at you. And you have taken your place as a proud, sovereign European nation, a vibrant democracy with a bright future ahead.” He said Europe owed a debt of gratitude to Ukraine for its fight. “I want to tell you something you probably don’t hear enough: thank you. Thank you all. Thank you. Thank you for the incredible stand you have taken because we are all stronger for it.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters after newsletter promotion Kyiv has said Russia is amassing more ballistic missiles and considering whether to mobilise an extra 300,000 soldiers. The missiles have been used to bomb Ukrainian infrastructure and warehouses, and to attack the capital, causing increased civilian casualties. There is a shortage of US-made Patriot interceptors, the only weapon that can effectively counter them. The UK has also announced it will help France set up assembly lines in Ukraine for long-range missiles, which the French president, Emmanuel Macron, promised last month. It has also previously announced that it will allow Ukraine to launch attacks with British-made drones, prompting warnings from Moscow that the UK will pay a “high price”. Russia has withdrawn its ambassador to the UK , with no replacement in sight. The long-serving ambassador, Andrey Kelin, left last month after seven years in post, according to the Russian embassy in London. A spokesperson said that relations had “deteriorated to an unprecedentedly low level entirely on London’s initiative”. A UK government spokesperson said the UK’s ambassador would continue in post in Moscow. Details of the Independence Day commemorations have not been made public amid fears of a Russian attack. Macron and the German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, will attend the coalition of the willing meeting by video link. Burnham travelled to Kyiv with the president of the European Council, António Costa, and the prime minister of Luxembourg, Luc Frieden. Volodymyr Zelenskyy is facing his biggest internal challenge after his former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov called for the country to hold elections for the first time since the war began. The Ukrainian president has said any poll risks splitting the country and would be “a tsunami for the state”. As part of a sabotage network coordinated from the Russian Federation, they were involved in an explosion and fire that occurred last month at an industrial facility in Brașov, in central Romania. The site is a subsidiary of Romarm, Romania’s main manufacturer of military equipment. Romanian judges have issued European arrest warrants against the individuals. According to DIICOT, two of the suspects were found and placed in pre-trial detention in Germany as they were preparing to carry out similar acts. On Monday, a third European arrest warrant was issued for another suspect, who had been located in Poland. Investigations are under way regarding the offence of attempted sabotage, and steps are being taken to have the 3 individuals extradited to Romania. DIICOT says the suspects also targeted other sites in Romania and other EU member states. In the current regional and European security climate, defined by a proliferation of hybrid warfare tactics, the evolution of asymmetric risks that could threaten public order or strategically important sites in Romania is monitored permanently, DIICOT said. The Romanian Intelligence Service also confirmed that the operations of the Moscow-coordinated sabotage network were not limited to Romania, but had an extensive list of targets in the region, including state-owned and private weapon production facilities, and other sites of military and industrial interest. Investigations conducted this year have uncovered further attempts targeting locations in Romania, including international military facilities or sites used for the training of Ukrainian armed forces, the SRI reports. According to the Service, such actions are intended to intimidate, to compromise defence capabilities, and to weaken the contribution of the targeted states to European and regional security. The SRI adds that recruitment typically takes place via social media. Those approached are initially offered money for specific, isolated tasks, such as observing or photographing certain sites. Over time, the assignments become increasingly serious, potentially escalating to acts of destruction, arson, or even assassination. These networks specifically exploit financial vulnerability, personal addictions, or a history of criminal activity. According to specialised agencies, Romania is not the only country targeted by acts of sabotage as part of the hybrid war waged by Russia in Europe. Germany, for instance, has recently seen a number of investigations and arrests linked to sabotage attempts targeting critical infrastructure, the energy grid, military sites, and international connections.
